units.translation: Thus I have emended for μεθεῖται [is let loose]. For after the words veόκοτα θρέομαι φοβερά μεγάλ᾽ ἄχη [I cry out fresh, fearful, great griefs] an ambiguous word is ineptly introduced, which seems to signify rather an army dismissed and going home than an army about to attack a city. Such an army should be said καθεῖσθαι [to be let down], as Herodotus said 7, 138 ή στρατηλασίη ή βασιλέος οὔνομα μὲν εἶχε ὡς ἐπ᾿ Ἀθήνας ἐλαύνοι, κατίετο δὲ ἐς πᾶσαν τὴν Ἑλλάδα [the expedition of the king had the name of marching against Athens, but was let loose upon all Greece]. and Polybius 3, 92, 7 εἰς δὲ τὸ πεδίον οὐ καθίει τὴν δύναμιν [he did not let his force down into the plain], to omit other examples of others. Moreover, that the prepositions κατά [down] and μετά [after, with] have very often been interchanged by scribes is known to everyone. Another example of this error is in Aeschylus in Ch.661 ὥρα δ᾽ ἐμπόρους μεθιέναι | ἄγκυραν ἐν δόμοισι πανδόκοις ξένων. ἄγκυραν μεθιέναι [it is time for merchants to let go the anchor in the all-receiving houses of strangers. To let go the anchor] whoever said this would mean that the anchor bound on the ship is loosed, evidently with the intention that it be fixed on the shore. But these roundabout ways of thinking did not please the Greeks, who clearly and briefly from Herodotus down to writers of the latest age said ἄγκυραν καθιέναι [to let down the anchor]. This therefore must be restored to Aeschylus too. Nor did the scholiast of Euripides on Orest. v. 54 say τὴν πλάτην μεθίεσθαι εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν [to let the oar go into the sea], which was read until now, but καθίεσθαι [to let down], which I restored from an ancient codex of the best note in the Oxford edition.
But I say that the bold transgressor will in time be brought low.
The army is let down, having left the camp.
I cry out fresh, fearful, great griefs
the expedition of the king had the name of marching against Athens, but was let loose upon all Greece
he did not let his force down into the plain
it is time for merchants to let go the anchor in the all-receiving houses of strangers. To let go the anchor
to let the oar go into the sea
Young, you will ride down the old woman's divinities.
A young man rides down me, an old woman.
You younger gods have ridden down the ancient laws.
aorist κατέστην [I stood, took my stand] I stand
And all night long they made the passage.
I am set as a guard of the land.
The army of the Greeks in no way made a secret sailing out.
Why do I delay to look upon the mind of Zeus?
May I not myself be taken by others and see my life.
to bring to anchor, bring into
Thus from the apograph: in M καθώρισας [you brought into], with the first letter changed to o by the same hand.
You have brought yourself into these calamities.
But the strength of god is still superior.
